question: Under what data, initialization, and training-time conditions do linear-model training trajectories occupy a low-dimensional hyper-ribbon in prediction space?

key_findings.claim: For full-batch linear regression, the covariance of residual trajectories decomposes into initialization, target, and cross terms whose spectra are controlled by the input Gram eigenvalues.
key_findings.evidence: The closed-form gradient-descent dynamics turn each input eigendirection into a different decay timescale, permitting eigenvalue bounds on the PCA matrix of trajectories.

key_findings.claim: A rapidly decaying input spectrum, target scale large relative to initialization, and an intermediate training horizon produce the narrowest predicted hyper-ribbons.
key_findings.evidence: Theorem 3 and phase diagrams separate regimes in slope, time, and target-to-weight scale; long training can add dimensions because slower modes enter the trajectory.

key_findings.claim: Kernel and stochastic-gradient extensions retain low-dimensionality only under additional spectral and noise assumptions.
key_findings.evidence: The kernel ensemble result uses interlacing/bounds over component kernels, while the SGD covariance gains a noise term whose Gram geometry can increase effective dimension.

method.core_idea: Explain an empirical low-dimensional prediction manifold by solving linear training dynamics and bounding the spectrum of its trajectory covariance.
method.mechanism: Diagonalize the input correlation operator, express residuals as mode-wise decays, decompose time-averaged covariance, and use Weyl/interlacing and displacement-rank arguments to identify phase boundaries.
assumptions: Squared-loss linear regression with a stable fixed step size is a meaningful mechanistic surrogate for deep-network prediction paths.
Inputs have an approximately geometric eigenspectrum and initial weights are isotropic.
PCA dimension of sampled trajectory points captures the information-geometric hyper-ribbon notion used by the motivating study.

techniques.role: Separates initialization, target and interaction contributions to prediction-space dimension.
Relates effective dimension to data-spectrum decay, target scale and training horizon.
Audits how ensembles and stochastic noise alter the same covariance geometry.

evaluations.setting: Synthetic linear regression across spectral slopes, initialization scales and horizons, with 100 initializations.
evaluations.metric: PCA eigenvalues and dimensions needed to explain the trajectory covariance.
evaluations.result: Numerical phase transitions follow the analytic bounds qualitatively.
evaluations.baseline: Direct eigendecomposition of simulated trajectories and the deep-network manifold phenomenon from prior work.

limitations: The main theorem is for linear squared-loss dynamics, not nonlinear feature learning.
Low-dimensional PCA in residual space is not identical to low-dimensionality under every information-geometric embedding.
Geometric data spectra and isotropic initialization are strong simplifying assumptions.
The bounds can be loose, as the observed displacement-rank decay is better than the proof uses.
failure_modes: Flat input spectra or long horizons activate many slow modes and widen the manifold.
Large SGD noise in nonsloppy directions can destroy the predicted ribbon.
A nonlinear network can change its kernel and leave the fixed-spectrum regime.
reusable_insights: Training-time horizon is part of any claimed intrinsic dimension, not merely a sampling detail.
Prediction-path dimension can often be separated into data geometry, target geometry, initialization and optimizer noise.
A solvable linear surrogate is strongest when its terms are mapped to falsifiable deep-network measurements.
open_questions: Do time-varying neural tangent kernels predict the same phase boundaries in deep networks?
Can the theory forecast manifold dimension before training from a real dataset spectrum?
How does adaptive optimization change the noise and mode timescales?

competitive_landscape.title: The Training Process of Many Deep Networks Explores the Same Low-Dimensional Manifold
competitive_landscape.relationship: Direct empirical precursor and motivating phenomenon.
competitive_landscape.difference: Mao et al. establish a shared prediction-space manifold across many deep models; the target analytically explains a linear analogue and isolates spectral phase controls.

competitive_landscape.title: Does the Data Induce Capacity Control in Deep Learning?
competitive_landscape.difference: Yang et al. connect sloppy input, Hessian/Fisher spectra, and generalization; the target focuses on the covariance of entire training trajectories and its time-dependent dimension.

competitive_landscape.title: Sloppiness and Emergent Theories in Physics, Biology, and Beyond
competitive_landscape.difference: The earlier work studies parameter sensitivities and emergent effective theories broadly; the target derives a supervised-learning trajectory result in prediction space.

novelty_assessment: The paper supplies a useful exact linear-model decomposition for a known deep-network manifold observation. Its novelty is the phase-boundary analysis, not discovery of sloppiness or low-dimensional training trajectories, and transfer to nonlinear representation learning remains conjectural.
reviewer_notes: Read all 15 extracted pages, including theorem proofs, phase plots, kernel/SGD extensions, and the discussion of looseness. Primary-source competitors were checked on 2026-08-23.
